article.title: I Miss You in Arabic, and the Vowel That Decides Who You Meant
article.excerpt: "I miss you" in Arabic is اشتقت إليك — ishtaqtu ilayka to a man, ilayki to a woman — and the mark that separates them is unwritten in all four Tatoeba sentences. What Egyptians send instead, what وحشتني literally means, and what 214 miss-you pages show about the letter around the line.

faqs.question: How do you write "I miss you" in Arabic?
faqs.answer: In Modern Standard Arabic it is اشتقت إليك, ishtaqtu ilayka to a man and ishtaqtu ilayki to a woman. Written without vowel marks, which is normal, both come out as the same eleven characters. Egyptians usually write وحشتني instead.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether a phrase I copied is the male or the female version?
faqs.answer: From the text alone, you usually cannot. The difference is U+064E ARABIC FATHA versus U+0650 ARABIC KASRA on the final kaf, and both are nonspacing marks that most writers omit — all four sentences with that phrase in the Tatoeba corpus leave them out. Say it aloud in a voice note and the ambiguity disappears.

faqs.question: What does وحشتني literally mean?
faqs.answer: Literally, "you have made me desolate". It is built on the root و ح ش, which Lane's lexicon glosses as wild animal, monster, and, of a place, destitute of human beings; Wiktionary defines the Egyptian verb waḥaš as "to cause longing". The person you miss is the grammatical subject, as in French tu me manques.

faqs.question: How do you say "I miss you" in Egyptian Arabic to a woman?
faqs.answer: وحشتيني, waḥaštīni, with an extra written ي before the object pronoun. The masculine is وحشتني, waḥaštini. This is one place where the dialect is clearer than the standard language — the gender is a full letter rather than an invisible mark.

faqs.question: Is اشتقت إليك too formal to text someone?
faqs.answer: It is not wrong, but it reads as written Arabic rather than spoken. Magidow's 2013 survey of 28 Damascene writers found native speakers actively steering between the two registers even inside formal writing. If you know the person's dialect, use it; if you do not, the standard form is the safe default.

faqs.question: What is the difference between اشتقت and أشتاق?
faqs.answer: أشتاق (ashtāqu) is the present and اشتقت (ishtaqtu) the perfect of the same form-VIII verb. Both are current for "I miss you" — Wiktionary's own usage examples use the present, while the Saudi autocomplete data is seeded on the perfect.

faqs.question: How is اشتقت إليك pronounced?
faqs.answer: ish-TAQ-tu i-LAY-ka to a man, ish-TAQ-tu i-LAY-ki to a woman, from the vocalised forms اِشْتَقْتُ إِلَيْكَ and اِشْتَقْتُ إِلَيْكِ. The whole gender distinction sits in that last syllable, which is why speaking it removes the guesswork that writing it introduces.

faqs.question: Can I use افتقدتك instead?
faqs.answer: Yes. افتقدتك is from a different root, افتقد, which Wiktionary glosses "to miss; to lose" and also "to examine; to study"; Tatoeba sentence 392779 translates it "I miss you". It reads cooler and more literary than اشتقت.

faqs.question: What do people say in the Gulf?
faqs.answer: The same verb with the object attached by لـ rather than إلى — اشتقت لك. Wiktionary's Hijazi entry gives the first-person past as aštagt and transliterates its own example اشتاقوا لك as one word, aštāgōlak.

faqs.question: Does it matter if I skip the vowel marks?
faqs.answer: For everyday messages, no — skipping them is standard practice, and every attested example in the corpora checked here skips them. It matters only when the gender is the point, and the fix is to say the line rather than type it.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Arabic, and the Vowel That Decides Who You Meant

"I miss you" in Arabic is اشتقت إليكَ (*ishtaqtu ilayka*) to a man and اشتقت إليكِ (*ishtaqtu ilayki*) to a woman. The two differ by one mark above or below the final letter, and that mark is almost never written — in all four sentences on Tatoeba containing that exact phrase, it is absent. So a line copied off a list carries no evidence of who it was meant for. Egyptians send a different sentence altogether, وحشتني, which puts the person you miss in the subject slot and says, literally, that they made you desolate. This page settles both against Lane's *Arabic-English Lexicon*, Wiktionary's paradigms and the Unicode character database, and adds what 214 pages built on the [SubhSandesh miss-you page](/missyou-gf) show about the message wrapped around the line: 43.5% of senders password-protect it before sharing, 93 of 214, the most private segment measured, and the median letter runs 88 words.

Transliterations follow the scheme Wiktionary's Arabic entries use — *ḥ* for ح, *š* for ش, long vowels as *ā ī ū* — except inside quotations, where each source's own romanisation stands.

## Why you cannot send this sentence without choosing a gender

The Arabic second-person suffix agrees with the person addressed, so there is no neutral "you" to attach. Wiktionary prints the pair on the entry for the verb itself: أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكَ tagged *to a man*, أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكِ tagged *to a woman*, same gloss for both.

Strip the vocalisation, as running text and phone keyboards do, and the two collapse into one string, إليك. The difference has moved into a mark that is no longer on the page.

Those marks have names and numbers. The masculine takes U+064E ARABIC FATHA and the feminine U+0650 ARABIC KASRA, and the [Unicode character database](https://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt) files both under general category Mn — nonspacing mark — inside the Arabic block U+0600–U+06FF. Nonspacing means zero advance width: the string takes the same room on screen with or without them.

Send اشتقت إليك to a man and it is correct; send the identical characters to a woman and it is also correct, and neither of you can tell from the text which you meant.

## What the verb actually says, and why "miss" is an approximation

[Wiktionary's entry for اشتاق](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D8%B4%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%82) — the page those two marked examples come from — files it as a form-VIII verb on the root ش و ق, built from the noun شَوْق, and glosses it "to yearn for" ahead of "to miss".

So the Arabic is about longing rather than about registering an absence, and English "miss" is an approximation in both directions. That also explains the two shapes you will see quoted: أشتاق إليك is the present, اشتقت إليك the perfect, and both are in use.

The same page carries the conjugation table, and that is where the second ambiguity lives. It gives اِشْتَقْتُ *ishtaqtu* "I", اِشْتَقْتَ *ishtaqta* "you (m.)" and اِشْتَقْتِ *ishtaqti* "you (f.)" — three different people, one written form, اشتقت. A two-word sentence hides two separate decisions.

Attested usage confirms it is normal to leave both open. All four Arabic sentences in the [Tatoeba corpus](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/392778) containing the exact string اشتقت إليك are written with no fatha and no kasra anywhere, and every English translation on them reads simply "I miss you".

## وحشتني, and why an Egyptian will not send you the standard line

Standard Arabic is what gets printed; it is not what gets typed into a chat. In Egypt the sentence is وحشتني, built on a different root with a much darker literal meaning.

Lane's entry for root [و ح ش](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2002.02.0041%3Aroot%3DwH%24) gives وَحْشٌ as "wild animal", "monster", and, of a place, "Desolate, deserted, or destitute of human beings". The form-IV verb اوحش الرَّجُلَ is "He made the man lonely, or solitary; and sad, sorrowful, or disquieted or troubled in mind; [by his absence]" — the opposite, Lane notes, of آنَسَهُ, to keep someone company. He then records the colloquial use himself: "Hence the saying of the people of Mekkeh, [and of Egypt,] أَوْحَشْتَنَا [Thou hast made us lonely, &c., by thine absence]."

That is the ancestor of the modern line, written down in the nineteenth century. Wiktionary's Egyptian entry for [وحش](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%88%D8%AD%D8%B4) defines the verb *waḥaš* as "to miss, to cause longing" — to *cause* it. So وحشتني parses as "you have made me desolate", with the missed person as grammatical subject, the way French *tu me manques* does.

Now the part nobody prints. Wiktionary's Egyptian conjugation table gives the past second person as وحشت *waḥašt* to a man and وحشتي *waḥašti* to a woman. Attach the object pronoun ـني and the form addressed to a woman gains a written ي, U+064A ARABIC LETTER YEH — a full letter, not a mark.

The dialect writes down the distinction that Modern Standard Arabic hides. That is the reverse of what learners are usually told, and it is the single most useful thing on this page.

## Four forms, and who each one is for

### 1. اشتقت إليكَ / إليكِ — Modern Standard Arabic

The written register: correspondence, captions, subtitles, anything formal. Attested four times on Tatoeba in that exact string, every one of them unvocalised. Safe everywhere and slightly bookish anywhere.

### 2. وحشتني (to a man) / وحشتيني (to a woman) — Egyptian

What an Egyptian actually sends. The masculine form is attested in Wiktionary's Hijazi example sentence وَحَشْتَنِي من زمان عنك, "I missed you, long time no see"; the feminine is read off the Egyptian conjugation table rather than from a headword of its own. Tatoeba's Arabic set returns zero sentences containing either string, which is what a corpus built on Modern Standard Arabic looks like.

### 3. اشتقت لك — Hijazi and the Gulf

The same form-VIII verb with the object attached by لـ rather than إلى. Wiktionary's Hijazi entry for اشتاق gives the first-person past *aštagt*, and its example اشتاقوا لك transliterates the preposition as a clitic, *aštāgōlak*.

### 4. افتقدتك — the other standard verb

A different root, افتقد, glossed on Wiktionary "to miss; to lose" and also "to examine; to study". Tatoeba sentence 392779, افتقدتك, is translated "I miss you". Cooler and more literary than اشتقت.

## How the line travels, and which channel keeps the vowel

Five ways the message reaches someone, against what 214 pages recorded between 2026-07-28 and 2026-09-25.

| How the line travels | Carries the gender vowel? | Measured across 214 miss-you pages |
|---|---|---|
| Typed into a chat, unvocalised | No — U+064E and U+0650 are dropped | Not measurable; letters are not language-tagged |
| Written letter on the page | No | Median 88 words, longest 1,024, n=214 |
| Voice note | Yes — *ilayka* and *ilayki* sound different | 13.6% record one (29 of 214) |
| Reunion countdown | Not applicable | 28.0% set a date (60 of 214) |
| Recipient's hug tap | Not applicable | 64.5% of pages got at least one (138 of 214); 1,434 taps, 512 on one page |

The takeaway is narrow and useful: of the five, only the voice note resolves the ambiguity, and only 29 of 214 senders used it.

Two disclosures that belong with those numbers. `viewCount` on the platform counts page views, not unique visitors, so the 2,417 views recorded on miss-you pages include the same recipient reopening a page. And the template has been live for two months at n=214, so nothing seasonal can be read out of it.

## What the search data measures, and what it does not

The keyword run behind this batch harvested Google autocomplete in nineteen markets. The Saudi Arabic market returned 40 suggestions; the US English market returned 1,216. That gap is not a measurement of Arabic demand — it is an artefact of the harvest script, which expands each seed with the Latin letters a–z, and every one of the 40 Arabic rows was produced by an English letter bolted onto اشتقت اليك.

So the Arabic-side evidence here is thin by construction. What did surface is still worth reporting: 21 of the 40 rows are people translating *out* of Arabic — into English, French, Spanish or Turkish — and 9 name a relative, including اشتقت اليك ابي رحمك الله, addressed to a dead father. Not one row contains وحش in any form, because the seed never gave it a chance to.

Native speakers find this hard too, which is the finding in [Alexander Magidow's 2013 study](https://journals.uio.no/JAIS/article/view/4631) in the *Journal of Arabic and Islamic Studies*. Surveying 28 native speakers of Damascene Arabic writing formal MSA, he found they avoid forms common in their own dialect even when those forms are perfectly correct in MSA — "negative interference", and part of why diglossia has lasted.

This page is the Arabic depth under the live hub on [saying I miss you in different languages](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages), which gives Arabic one line. It does not repeat that table; it adds the vowel mechanics, the dialect inversion and the corpus counts.

## When Arabic is the wrong choice, and when a page is

If your recipient reads Arabic but the two of you speak English to each other, sending the line untranslated reads as a performance rather than a message. Write the letter in the language you actually share and let the Arabic be one line inside it.

A page is the wrong instrument too, in two specific cases. Nine of the 40 Arabic rows in the harvest name a parent and one marks that parent as dead — for that reader a reunion countdown is worse than nothing, and a [photo jigsaw whose last piece is not in the box](/photo-puzzle) carries a letter without promising a date. And if the recipient is in the same room, just say it.

One more limit on our own numbers: the city, background-music and "together since" fields on the miss-you page are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates describe the form, not the sender. Only the password, the voice note, the reunion date, the letter and the memories are genuine choices, and those are the only ones quoted above.

## Sources

- [Edward William Lane, *An Arabic-English Lexicon*, root و ح ش](https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2002.02.0041%3Aroot%3DwH%24) — Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University. Published 1863–1893.
- [Wiktionary, وحش](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%88%D8%AD%D8%B4) — Egyptian Arabic verb *waḥaš*, its conjugation table, and the Hijazi example sentence.
- [Wiktionary, اشتاق](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D8%B4%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%82) — form-VIII verb, the two gender-marked examples, and the Modern Standard Arabic conjugation.
- [Tatoeba, sentence 392778](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/392778) — attested Arabic sentences and their English translations, CC BY 2.0 FR.
- [The Unicode Character Database, UnicodeData.txt](https://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt) — Unicode Consortium.
- [Alexander Magidow, "Competing Pressures in Diglossia: Avoiding Colloquial Elements in Writing Modern Standard Arabic"](https://journals.uio.no/JAIS/article/view/4631) — *Journal of Arabic and Islamic Studies* 13, 2013.

A search of the Arabic set returns zero sentences containing وحشتني or وحشني. Sentence 392779, افتقدتك, is also translated "I miss you".
064E;ARABIC FATHA;Mn and 0650;ARABIC KASRA;Mn — both nonspacing marks; 064A;ARABIC LETTER YEH;Lo and 0643;ARABIC LETTER KAF;Lo are letters. Blocks.txt gives 0600..06FF; Arabic.

A multiple-choice survey of 28 native speakers of Damascene Arabic writing formal Modern Standard Arabic found they "tend to avoid elements that are common in their local colloquial dialect, even if they are attested and permissible in Modern Standard Arabic" — negative interference — which the author argues helps explain the historical robustness of diglossia.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this SERP that names U+064E and U+0650, counts how often attested Arabic writes them (zero of the four Tatoeba sentences carrying the phrase), and pairs that with Lane's own record of أوحشتنا as Egyptian usage — which turns وحشتني from a dialect curiosity into the older, more literal way of saying it. The claim an answer engine has most reason to lift is the one nobody else states: for this sentence the dialect is the precise one, because Egyptian marks a female addressee with a written ي while Modern Standard Arabic hides it in a mark nobody types. What it cannot overcome: the competing results are Arabic-teaching domains with years of topical links, while subhsandesh.in is a gifting site with no Arabic authority at all, and the demand behind the keyword is small — `i miss you in arabic` surfaced in one market of nineteen. Ranking, if it happens, takes months.

structuralLimitations: BRIEF §0 CORRECTION — the prompt gave the Egyptian form as "وحشتني (waḥashtīni)". Those two do not match. Wiktionary's Egyptian conjugation table for وحش gives the past second person as وحشت (waḥašt) to a man and وحشتي (waḥašti) to a woman, so the string وحشتني is the form addressed to a MAN (waḥašt + ni), while the transliteration waḥaštīni belongs to وحشتيني, addressed to a woman. The post prints both, correctly paired, and makes the mismatch into its best claim: the Egyptian feminine adds a written ي (U+064A), so the dialect writes down the very distinction the prompt says Modern Standard Arabic hides.

BRIEF §0 CORRECTION — the prompt gave the two MSA forms as اشتقت إليكَ / إليكِ only. Wiktionary's own usage examples on the اشتاق entry use the PRESENT, أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكَ / إِلَيْكِ, and so does the single Arabic line on the live hub (id 1360). Both tenses are current; the post says so rather than presenting the perfect as the only form. The autocomplete harvest happens to be seeded on the perfect, which is why the Arabic rows all show اشتقت.

BRIEF §0 EXTENSION, VERIFIED — the prompt says the gender is hidden in one unwritten vowel. It is worse than that. The verb اشتقت is itself three different people in Wiktionary's paradigm — اِشْتَقْتُ ištaqtu "I", اِشْتَقْتَ ištaqta "you (m.)", اِشْتَقْتِ ištaqti "you (f.)" — all spelled اشتقت unvocalised. A two-word sentence carries two separate unwritten decisions, not one.

PROMPT CLAIM CONFIRMED AND QUANTIFIED — the Arabic harvest really is broken on the Arabic side, and the mechanism is visible in the data. content/keywords/2026-09-25-miss-you-global/ac/sa-ar/autocomplete.csv holds exactly 40 rows against 1,216 for us-en, and every row's source_prefixes column is the seed اشتقت اليك followed by a LATIN letter (a, b, e, f, g, i, m, p, t, or the bigram "in"). No Arabic letter ever expanded the stem. Consequences the post states rather than hides: not one of the 40 rows contains وحش in any form, because the seed never gave it a chance to appear; 21 of the 40 are people translating OUT of Arabic into English, French, Spanish or Turkish; and 9 name a relative, including اشتقت اليك ابي رحمك الله, addressed to a dead father.

ENGLISH-SIDE DEMAND, MEASURED — the post's own keyword is an English query and is unaffected by the Arabic harvest problem, but it is small. `i miss you in arabic` surfaced in us-en only (2 prefix hits, best rank 10); `miss you in arabic` in gb-en and us-en (4 prefix hits); `what's i miss you in arabic` in in-en and us-en. The harvest also shows `miss kita in arabic` from ph-en and `aku rindu kamu in arabic` from id-id — people reaching Arabic from a third language.

LINE CUT 1 — Tunisian توحّشتك (twa7achtik), which the SERP offered. Wiktionary's توحش entry has no Tunisian section and no "miss" sense at all in Modern Standard Arabic ("to be unsocial", "to act wild", "to be desolate"). Cut rather than printed on a search snippet's authority.
LINE CUT 2 — Moroccan Darija اشتئتلك (ishta'telak). No fetched dictionary entry supports it; Wiktionary has no Moroccan section on اشتاق.

LINE CUT 3 — "Levantine وحشتني". The prompt offered وحشتني as a Levantine option alongside اشتقتلك. The fetched entries do not support it: Wiktionary's South Levantine اشتاق (ištāʔ) gives حنّ (ḥann) as its synonym, not وحش, and the وحش page carries Egyptian and Hijazi sections only. The post assigns وحشتني to Egypt, where a fetched source puts it.

LINE CUT 4 — اشتقتلك written as one word. There is no Wiktionary entry for that string, and the Hijazi example on the اشتاق page writes the preposition separately (اشتاقوا لك) while transliterating it as a clitic. The post prints اشتقت لك and explains the clitic rather than printing the unattested spelling as a phrase to send.

LINE CUT 5 — أفتقدك (aftaqiduka), which the SERP offered as an alternative spelling of the same idea. It is a different verb, and the corpus attests the perfect افتقدتك (Tatoeba 392779, "I miss you"), not the imperfect. The post prints the attested form and notes that the root's other sense is "to examine; to study".

LINE CUT 6 — the authorship of اشتقت إليك فعلمني ألا أشتاق, which accounts for 7 of the 40 Arabic harvest rows and which one row attributes to نزار. No fetched source confirms the attribution, so the poem is not named or quoted in the post.
LINE CUT 7 — "وحشتني means I miss you very much". The intensifier is in the SERP gloss and not in the morphology; the verb carries no degree marker. Cut.

LINE CUT 8 — labelling اشتقت لك as "Gulf". The fetched Wiktionary evidence is for HIJAZI (code acw), which is western Saudi Arabia, not the Gulf. The heading says "Hijazi and the Gulf" and the body attributes the paradigm to the Hijazi entry only.

SOURCE CUT, AND WHY — Lane's entry for root ش و ق was fetched and read in full (https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2002.02.0027%3Aroot%3D%24wq). It glosses اشتاق إليه "He was, or became, desirous of it; or affected with desire for it; [or he yearned or longed for it in his soul]" and شَوْقٌ as "Desire, or yearning or longing of the soul", and its form-I شَاقَنِى is itself inverted ("It ... excited my desire"), which would have shown that the وحشتني inversion has a classical parallel. It was cut from `sources` to stay inside the 4–6 cap, and the "longing, not missing" claim was re-sourced to Wiktionary's اشتاق entry, which carries the same ordering of senses. The claim about شَاقَنِى does not appear in the post at all.

PEER-REVIEWED SOURCE, AND WHAT IT COST — findpapers.mjs was run on `Arabic diglossia dialect standard`, `gender agreement Arabic second person` and `Arabic dialect emotion expression`. The closest paper to this post's angle was Asadi & Ibrahim, "Diglossia and Orthographic Complexity as Multiplicative but not Additive Challenges in Arabic" (J Psycholinguist Res, doi:10.1007/s10936-026-10214-3, PMC13050341) — diglossia AND the missing short vowels, exactly this page's two problems. The PMC family was at the 3-post batch cap, and both publisher copies (link.springer.com, www.nature.com for the Scientific Reports alternative) served a JavaScript bot challenge instead of text, so neither could be read or cited. Magidow 2013 in the Journal of Arabic and Islamic Studies was substituted: peer-reviewed, open access, readable, on a domain at zero posts, and genuinely about diglossia — but about what Damascene writers avoid, not about orthography. That is a real loss and it is recorded here rather than papered over.

SOURCES UNREACHABLE — almaany.com returned HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare challenge on all three lookups attempted (اشتقت, وحشتني, شوق), so no modern-usage claim in this post rests on it. lexicon.quranicarabic.com is a parked domain for sale, not a lexicon. arabiclexicon.hawramani.com returned a database error. archive.org's Lane scans require JavaScript. Lane was reached instead through the Perseus Digital Library at Tufts, which serves the 1863–1893 edition as text, split by letter, and both root entries used here were fetched and read.

CAP-EXEMPT DOMAINS USED — en.wiktionary.org, tatoeba.org and unicode.org, all listed in verify.config.json capExemptDomains. All three were fetched (Wiktionary via the MediaWiki parse API for both wikitext and the rendered conjugation tables; Tatoeba via api_v0 search paged to exhaustion for four query strings; unicode.org via UnicodeData.txt and Blocks.txt) and each verified to contain what is attributed to it. capcheck.mjs was re-run immediately before saving: perseus.tufts.edu and journals.uio.no are both at zero posts, and this post touches neither europepmc.org/pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov nor doi.org.

FIRST-PARTY LIMIT — /missyou-gf letter text is free input and is not language-tagged, so the platform cannot say whether any of the 214 senders wrote a word of Arabic. Every first-party number in the post is about the CHANNEL — password, letter length, voice note, reunion date, hug taps — never about the language, and the comparison table says so in its own first column.

WHAT THIS DOES THAT THE HUB DOES NOT — the live hub /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages (Strapi id 1360) gives Arabic one line: "Arabic: أشتاق إليك (ash-taaq ilayk / ash-taaq ilayki)", plus a general note that Arabic "changes verbs based on gender or formality". It never says which mark makes the difference, never mentions that the mark is normally absent, and never mentions a dialect. Its table is not restated here. This page adds the codepoints, the corpus counts, Lane on the و ح ش root, the Egyptian inversion, the four-form comparison and the first-party channel data.

CANNIBALISATION — no live Strapi slug contains "arabic" (queried 2026-09-25), and none of the 81 live "miss" slugs is a translation spoke for a Semitic language. On the BRIEF's three-axis test this differs on the LANGUAGE axis from every one of them. No merge recommended.

SERP, AS ACTUALLY RUN — one WebSearch on the exact keyword returned, in order: arabic.fi (a sentence database), blog.alifbee.com, quora.com, two wordhippo.com pages, earabic.io, ithacaboundlanguages.com, and two Wikipedia articles about songs titled "I Miss You". No page on that SERP was fetched, linked, cited or paraphrased, per references/competitors.md, and no claim is made here about their word counts, headings or schema, because none was measured. The search result summary itself contained two things this post corrects: it glossed أفتقدك as a pronunciation of اشتقت إليك (a different root), and it glossed وحشتني as "I miss you very much".
